```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaFin)
```

Can the lasso help analyze a single stock? This article walks through one
concrete, reproducible example. The goal is **sparse signal attribution** —
finding the few signals, out of many candidates, that explain a stock's
next-day return — not reliable price prediction. Daily equity returns have a
very low signal-to-noise ratio, so any edge is small; the honest result below
is a modest one, and half the lesson is validating it correctly.

Two rules matter more than the solver:

- **Respect the time order.** Fit only on past data. Random K-fold
  cross-validation leaks the future into the training fold and is
  inappropriate for time series.
- **Freeze preprocessing on the training window.** Standardize features
  using training statistics only, then apply that fixed transform forward.

`cudaFin::rolling_predict()` implements exactly this pattern: it refits a
lasso on each rolling window and forms one-step-ahead forecasts. Everything
below uses only `cudaFin` and base R — no `glmnet`, no `cudaGlmnet`, no extra
dependencies — which keeps the example (and the package) lightweight.

## A simulated single stock

We simulate about 1.5 years of daily data: 30 candidate signals on a common
scale (already standardized by construction, so no fitted preprocessing is
needed here). Only the first three drive the return, with coefficients 0.9,
-0.6 and 0.4; the other 27 are noise. The noise is scaled so the in-sample
R-squared is about 0.10 — deliberately low, like real equity returns.
Features observed at the close of day `t` predict the return of day `t + 1`,
so the design matrix is lagged by one row.

```{r data}
set.seed(42)
n_days <- 420L
p <- 30L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n_days * p), n_days, p)
beta_true <- c(0.9, -0.6, 0.4, rep(0, p - 3L))
signal <- drop(X %*% beta_true)
noise <- rnorm(n_days, sd = sqrt(var(signal) * (1 / 0.10 - 1)))
ret <- c(NA, signal[seq_len(n_days - 1L)] + noise[2:n_days])
X <- X[seq_len(n_days - 1L), , drop = FALSE]
y <- ret[2:n_days]
c(n = nrow(X), p = ncol(X), true_drivers = sum(beta_true != 0))
```

## The estimator and a transparent reference

`rolling_predict()` minimizes squared error plus an L1 penalty by proximal
gradient (ISTA), with a fixed step size and a fixed number of iterations on
each window. That is a *truncated* solve: coefficients are a lightly
regularized approximation, not the fully converged optimum. This is fine here
because we care about walk-forward errors and the sparsity pattern, not exact
coefficient values.

For the sweeps below we use `roll_lasso()`, a short pure-R implementation of
the same deterministic contract (fixed step `1 / sum(Xw^2)`, soft threshold
`lambda * window * step`). It is exactly what the package tests mirror
`rolling_predict()` against, and the getting-started vignette uses the same
reference. Keeping the computation in plain R makes the article fast and
reproducible on any backend; the last section verifies that
`rolling_predict()` returns identical numbers to machine precision.

```{r reference}
roll_lasso <- function(X, y, window, lambda, n_iter) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)
  np <- n - window
  pred <- numeric(np)
  actual <- numeric(np)
  coef <- matrix(0, p, np)
  for (tt in (window + 1L):n) {
    slot <- tt - window
    rows <- (tt - window):(tt - 1L)
    Xw <- X[rows, , drop = FALSE]
    yw <- y[rows]
    step <- 1 / sum(Xw^2)
    thresh <- lambda * window * step
    beta <- rep(0, p)
    for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
      r <- (yw - as.vector(Xw %*% beta)) * step
      u <- beta + as.vector(crossprod(Xw, r))
      beta <- sign(u) * pmax(abs(u) - thresh, 0)
    }
    pred[slot] <- sum(X[tt, ] * beta)
    actual[slot] <- y[tt]
    coef[, slot] <- beta
  }
  list(pred = pred, actual = actual, coef = coef,
       mse = mean((pred - actual)^2),
       dir_acc = mean(sign(pred) == sign(actual)))
}
```

## Choosing the penalty on the training period only

We split at row 280: rows 1-280 are the training/validation period used to
choose `lambda`; rows 281 onward are locked away as an out-of-sample test.
Each `roll_lasso()` fit is itself walk-forward — the forecast for row
`window + i` is fit only on the trailing `window` rows — so no future row ever
enters a fit. We pick `lambda` by minimizing walk-forward MSE on the training
period alone.

```{r selection-setup}
train_end <- 280L
window <- 120L
n_iter <- 100L
grid <- c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.2)
Xtr <- X[seq_len(train_end), , drop = FALSE]
ytr <- y[seq_len(train_end)]
```

```{r train-sweep}
tr_mse <- vapply(grid, function(l) {
  roll_lasso(Xtr, ytr, window, l, n_iter)$mse
}, numeric(1))
tr_nz <- vapply(grid, function(l) {
  f <- roll_lasso(Xtr, ytr, window, l, n_iter)
  mean(colSums(f$coef != 0))
}, numeric(1))
sweep <- rbind(train_mse = round(tr_mse, 3),
               mean_nonzero = round(tr_nz, 2))
colnames(sweep) <- grid
sweep
```

As `lambda` grows, fewer features survive and the error first falls (noise is
pruned) then rises (real signal is pruned too). The minimum is at the value
below; we lock it now and do not look at the test period until the next
section.

```{r chosen-lambda}
best <- grid[which.min(tr_mse)]
best
```

## Honest out-of-sample results

We now run the full series at the locked penalty and score only forecasts
whose target row is past `train_end`. The natural benchmark for a single
stock's return is the **zero-return forecast** (predict the mean, about zero);
beating it in mean squared error is already a real, if modest, result. We also
report direction accuracy against a 0.50 coin-flip reference, and compare an
unpenalized fit that keeps all 30 features.

```{r oos-fn}
oos <- function(lambda) {
  f <- roll_lasso(X, y, window, lambda, n_iter)
  keep <- (window + seq_along(f$pred)) > train_end
  pred <- f$pred[keep]
  actual <- f$actual[keep]
  list(mse = mean((pred - actual)^2),
       dir_acc = mean(sign(pred) == sign(actual)),
       mean_nz = mean(colSums(f$coef[, keep, drop = FALSE] != 0)),
       sel = rowMeans(f$coef[, keep, drop = FALSE] != 0),
       n_oos = length(actual))
}
zero <- mean(y[(train_end + 1L):nrow(X)]^2)
o <- oos(best)
o0 <- oos(0)
mse_gain <- 100 * (zero - o$mse) / zero
```

```{r oos-table}
data.frame(
  model = c("zero return", "unpenalized (lambda = 0)",
            sprintf("lasso (locked lambda = %s)", best)),
  oos_mse = round(c(zero, o0$mse, o$mse), 3),
  dir_acc = round(c(NA, o0$dir_acc, o$dir_acc), 3),
  mean_nonzero = round(c(0, o0$mean_nz, o$mean_nz), 1)
)
cat("OOS observations:", o$n_oos, "\n")
cat("MSE reduction vs zero:", sprintf("%.1f%%", mse_gain), "\n")
```

At the locked penalty the lasso reaches an out-of-sample MSE about 6.5% lower
than the zero-return forecast, with direction accuracy around 0.58 versus the
0.50 coin flip. The unpenalized fit retains all 30 features and does worse
out-of-sample than the sparse lasso — the classic sign that regularization is
pruning noise rather than signal here. These are thin edges, which is exactly
what to expect at R-squared about 0.10.

The plot below is a **retrospective diagnostic computed after locking**
`lambda`; it is not used to choose anything. It shows the out-of-sample
optimum is broad and sits slightly below the training-chosen value. At this
signal-to-noise ratio the tuning is noisy — another reason to prefer a simple,
moderately penalized model over fine-tuning.

```{r oos-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
oos_mse <- vapply(grid, function(l) oos(l)$mse, numeric(1))
plot(grid, oos_mse, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "lambda", ylab = "Out-of-sample MSE",
     main = "Diagnostic only: OOS error vs penalty")
abline(h = zero, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
points(best, oos(best)$mse, pch = 17, col = "darkorange", cex = 1.5)
text(best, oos(best)$mse, labels = "locked", pos = 4, cex = 0.8,
     col = "darkorange")
```

## What the lasso actually selected

Averaged over the out-of-sample windows, the three true drivers (features 1,
2, 3) dominate, while most noise features appear only occasionally.

```{r selection-freq}
round(o$sel[1:6], 2)
cat("mean selection freq, noise features 4-30:",
    round(mean(o$sel[4:30]), 3), "\n")
```

```{r selection-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
barplot(o$sel, names.arg = seq_along(o$sel),
        col = ifelse(o$sel > 0.5, "darkorange", "grey70"),
        xlab = "Feature", ylab = "Selection frequency",
        main = "How often each feature survives (OOS windows)")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

Feature 3 has the weakest true signal and appears about half the time, and a
couple of noise features flicker in. That is the realistic picture at low
signal-to-noise: the lasso concentrates weight on the real drivers but does
not give a perfectly clean indicator.

## A complication: collinear signals

Real candidate signals are correlated. Make feature 4 an exact copy of
feature 1, then refit:

```{r collinearity}
X_col <- X
X_col[, 4L] <- X[, 1L]
fc <- roll_lasso(X_col, y, window, best, n_iter)
keepc <- (window + seq_along(fc$pred)) > train_end
c(driver_1 = round(mean(fc$coef[1L, keepc]), 3),
  duplicate_4 = round(mean(fc$coef[4L, keepc]), 3))
```

The fitted weight splits almost evenly between the two identical columns.
Neither is "more causal": the lasso cannot distinguish collinear candidates
and simply shares the weight between them. So a non-zero coefficient is
evidence of association, not of a causal driver — with correlated real-world
signals, do not over-interpret which feature was selected.

## Equivalence to the compiled function

Finally, confirm that `cudaFin::rolling_predict()` agrees with the reference.
On a small case the forecasts and coefficients match to about 1e-15 — pure
floating-point round-off between the CPU and GPU linear-algebra backends. In
production you would call `rolling_predict()` directly; it is the same
computation, and the package test suite holds it to this contract on both
backends.

```{r equivalence}
idx <- seq_len(90L)
w_chk <- 60L
ni_chk <- 30L
Xs <- X[idx, , drop = FALSE]
ys <- y[idx]
chk <- rolling_predict(Xs, ys, window = w_chk, lambda = 0.3,
                       n_iter = ni_chk)
ref <- roll_lasso(Xs, ys, w_chk, 0.3, ni_chk)
cat(sprintf("backend: %s\n", chk$backend))
cat(sprintf("max |pred - ref| = %.3g\n",
            max(abs(chk$pred - ref$pred))))
cat(sprintf("max |coef - ref| = %.3g\n",
            max(abs(chk$coefficients - ref$coef))))
```

## Caveats and takeaways

- This is synthetic data. Real single-stock daily returns have even lower
  signal-to-noise; a 6% MSE edge here is illustrative, not a trading result.
- No transaction costs, turnover limits, or regime changes are modeled.
- The solve is truncated (fixed ISTA steps), so coefficients are approximate.
- Standardize on the training window only; we skipped fitting it here merely
  because the simulated features already share a scale.
- Collinear signals make the selected set non-unique; selection is not
  causation.
- Tune `lambda` on a time-ordered validation period and lock it before
  touching the test period; random K-fold CV is inappropriate here.
- Direction accuracy above 0.50 is the bar, and the margin here is thin.

`cudaFin` keeps this whole example dependency-light: the only package used is
`cudaFin` itself, plus base R.
